h1: Picking typefaces for a brewery identity that stay legible on a shelf
title: Brewery Typefaces That Read on a Shelf | Craft Beer School
desc: How to choose typefaces for a brewery brand that stay readable on curved cans, small labels, tap lists and phone screens, with tests to run before you commit.
teaser: If a shopper cannot read the beer's name from a metre away, the most beautiful lettering in the world has failed.
standfirst: Type does more work on a beer pack than any illustration. It names the beer, states the style and carries the legal text. Here is how we pick typefaces that look like the brand and still read on a crowded shelf.
sections: Type has two jobs on a beer pack

The first job is character. A brewery's wordmark and display type tell a shopper whether this is a playful brewpub, a serious lager house or a hop-forward upstart before they read a single word. The second job is plain reading: beer name, style, ABV, volume, legal text, the batch date.

Most legibility problems come from asking one typeface to do both. A hand-drawn display face that looks great at 40 mm tall becomes unreadable at 2 mm. Pick a display face for character and a separate workhorse face for information. Keep the second one boring on purpose.
What makes a face readable small

• Generous x-height. Lowercase letters that are tall relative to capitals stay open when printed small.
  • Open shapes. Letters like a, e, c and s should have clear openings that ink cannot fill in.
  • Even stroke weight. Very thin strokes break up on metal and on uncoated paper. Hairline serifs vanish.
  • Clear figures. 1, 7, 3 and 8 must be easy to tell apart, because ABV, volume and dates are numbers. A 4.5% beer read as 4.8% is a small problem. A misread date code is a bigger one.

Condensed faces save width, which is tempting on a narrow can, but very condensed bold type closes up under print gain. Test before you commit.

A can bends type away from the eye. Long words set across the full face lose their ends round the side. Keep the beer name short enough to sit within the visible strip, or stack it on two lines. Vertical type running up the can is fashionable and hard to read in a fridge, so keep it for decoration, not names.

On a shelf the shopper is usually a metre or two away. As a rough working check, print the name at true size, stand two metres back and see whether you can read it without leaning in. If not, go bigger or bolder. Our guide to beer label design covers how hierarchy on the face supports this.

If your brand uses Devanagari, Kannada, Tamil or another script alongside English, choose families designed to work together, with matching weights and similar visual size. Many Latin display faces have no matching Indian script. A mismatched pairing looks like an afterthought. Some states may also ask for label text in the local language, so plan the space even if you do not use it on day one. Check the current requirement with your licensing consultant.

Fonts are software with licences. A free download may not allow commercial packaging. A desktop licence may not cover use on a website or app. Buy the licence that covers print, web and merchandise, keep the receipt with the brand files and give your designer and printer the same files. When a printer substitutes a font because yours was not embedded, the ABV line often shifts first.

Write the type rules into the brand book: which face for names, which for body, minimum sizes, letter spacing for the wordmark. Without rules, every new label drifts.

Type that works on a can may not work on a chalkboard, a printed menu or a TV tap list. Bars are dim and lit with warm bulbs. People read menus from across a table. Use the workhorse face at a generous size for beer names and prices. On screens, check the web version of your fonts on a cheap Android phone in sunlight, because that is how many people in India will first see your beer.

A detail from the taproom floor: the tap list is read by staff as much as by drinkers, often in a rush. If two beer names look alike in your chosen face, staff will pour the wrong one. Short, distinct names set in clear type save more pints than any training session.

1. Print the full can or label at true size on the real material.
  2. Read the ABV, volume and date from arm's length under shop lighting.
  3. Read the beer name from two metres.
  4. Photograph it on a phone and view it at thumbnail size.

Each of these takes a few minutes. Skipping them can cost a full reprint, plus another round of label approval in states that require one.
faqs: Should a brewery use one typeface or two?
Usually two: a display face with character for names and a plain, readable face for information. Some brands add a third for a hand-drawn wordmark, but rules matter more than the count.
Can I use a free font on my cans?
Only if its licence allows commercial packaging. Check the licence for print, web and merchandise use before the artwork is final.
What size should the text on a can be?
Legal text has minimum sizes set by regulation, so confirm those first. Beyond that, test real prints at arm's length and two metres rather than trusting a screen.
